opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think we've badly underrated it for a long time. There's this persistent idea that humans have a weak sense of smell, that we're a "visual species" and smell is a vestigial leftover. A lot of that traces back to the 19th century, when anatomists noticed our olfactory bulbs are small relative to the rest of our brain and concluded the sense itself must be poor. That doesn't hold up. In absolute terms our olfactory bulbs have roughly as many neurons as those of many mammals we think of as great smellers. And when you actually test people, they can follow scent trails across a field, pick out family members by body odor, and detect some compounds at parts-per-trillion concentrations, which is competitive with dogs and rodents for certain molecules.

On the hardware side, we have around 400 functional olfactory receptor types. Compare that with vision, where color comes down to three cone types. Smell is a combinatorial code: any given molecule activates a pattern across many of those receptors, and the brain reads the pattern. So the space of things we can potentially distinguish is enormous. You may have seen the estimate that people can tell apart a trillion odors. That specific number has been debated, and I wouldn't hang my hat on it, but the broad point holds that the discriminable space is vast.

Where it gets interesting is the difference between detection and discrimination on one side, and naming and description on the other. People are often surprisingly good at noticing that two smells differ and surprisingly bad at saying what they are. Hand someone a jar of something completely familiar, like cinnamon or coffee, with no context, and many people struggle to name it. That isn't a failure of the nose. It reflects how little we train the link between smell and language. Perfumers, flavorists, and sommeliers show that with practice that link becomes very rich.

That gap is a big part of why we did the work we did on building an odor map. If you want to measure what humans can perceive, you need a consistent way to describe it. So we worked with trained panelists who rated molecules on a fixed vocabulary of descriptors, things like "fruity," "woody," "garlic," and so on, and then asked whether a model could predict those ratings from molecular structure. One of the results I'm proudest of is that the model's predictions were, on average, closer to the panel consensus than a typical individual panelist was. That tells you two things. Human perception of smell is structured and reproducible enough to be learned. And individual humans vary quite a bit, partly because of genetics, since people carry different variants of their receptors, and partly because of experience.

So my short answer is that the human sense of smell is far more capable than we give it credit for. What's mostly lacking is the measurement infrastructure and the shared language. For vision we have RGB and for sound we have frequency, so we can digitize them. Smell has never had that, and building it is really the frontier.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the human sense of smell is dramatically underrated, and that's kind of a cultural thing more than a biological thing. There's this old idea, going back to Aristotle and running through Freud and a lot of Western thought, that smell is a lesser sense, something more primitive, something we kind of left behind when we stood up on two legs and started relying on vision. And if you actually look at the data, that just doesn't hold up.

A few things I'd point to. One, in terms of raw discriminative power, there was a study out of Rockefeller a number of years ago that estimated humans can distinguish something on the order of a trillion different odor stimuli. You can argue about the exact number, and people have, but even if it's off by orders of magnitude, it's an enormous space. Compare that to vision, where we talk about a few million colors, or hearing, where it's maybe hundreds of thousands of distinguishable tones. Smell is high-dimensional in a way the other senses aren't.

Two, we're actually quite sensitive. For certain molecules, humans can detect concentrations of a few parts per trillion, and there are compounds where we outperform dogs. Dogs are better at tracking and sampling, they have the nose-to-the-ground behavior and the anatomy, but molecule for molecule it's not the blowout people assume. There's a nice experiment from Noam Sobel's lab where they had undergraduates get down on all fours and follow a scent trail across a field, and they could do it, and they got better with practice.

So where does the weakness come from? I'd say it's mostly on the language and attention side, not the receptor side. We have about 400 functional olfactory receptor types, which is a lot, more than any other sensory system. But we have almost no vocabulary for odors. Most people can only name a handful of smells when they're presented blind, even very familiar ones. We describe smells by referring to their source, "it smells like coffee," rather than having abstract descriptors the way we have "red" or "loud." And that bottleneck between perception and language makes us feel like we're bad at it, when really we're just bad at talking about it.

And the last thing I'd say, which is the part I find most interesting from a machine learning perspective, is that smell is the sense we understand least at a fundamental level. We can look at a wavelength of light and predict what color you'll see. We can look at a frequency and predict the pitch. We can't look at a molecule's structure and reliably predict what it smells like. That structure-to-percept map is still largely unsolved. So the capability is there in humans, it's just that both our introspective access to it and our scientific understanding of it lag way behind the other senses.

astra-6.text:
I think we tend to underestimate it. We tell ourselves that humans are visual creatures and that dogs are the ones with a great sense of smell. But when you actually test people, we're remarkably sensitive to certain odors. There isn't one universal ranking of who has the best nose—it depends on the molecule and the task.

What we're often bad at is naming what we smell. You can recognize an odor, or have it immediately bring back a memory, without being able to say what it is. And I think we confuse that difficulty putting smells into words with an inability to perceive them. Those are very different things.

r001.rationale: It says there is no universal ranking of who has the best nose, but does not state that the number of distinct smells humans can perceive is unknown.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes perceiving or recognizing an odor from naming it, but does not distinguish odor detection from discriminating subtle differences between odors.

r003.rationale: It does not mention humans following a scent trail.

r004.rationale: It describes sensitivity generally but gives no parts-per-billion or parts-per-trillion concentration claim.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the human sense of smell is vastly underappreciated. We tend to think of ourselves as visual creatures and assume that dogs and other animals live in this rich world of odors that we can barely access. But humans are actually remarkably good at certain smell tasks. We can distinguish an enormous range of odors, and we can detect some molecules at incredibly low concentrations.

What we’re less good at is describing what we smell. You can recognize a smell immediately, and it might bring back a vivid memory, but naming it can be surprisingly difficult. That gap between what our noses can perceive and what we can put into words makes the sense itself seem less capable than it really is.
